blocks.text:
### Real-world problems and solutions

#### Incident: commit latency high because every commit waits for fsync

**Scenario.** An order service performs one small transaction per HTTP request. After a migration to a cloud volume, the 99th percentile latency of writes rises from 3 ms to 40 ms although CPU and queries are unchanged.

**Symptoms.** `pg_stat_activity` shows many sessions with `wait_event = WALSync` or `WALWrite`; throughput saturates at a few hundred commits per second.

**Diagnosis.**

1. Sample wait events: `SELECT wait_event_type, wait_event, count(*) FROM pg_stat_activity WHERE state =` `'active' GROUP BY 1, 2 ORDER BY 3 DESC;`. A dominance of `IO / WALSync` points to the log flush.
2. Measure the device: `pg_test_fsync -f /path/on/the/wal/volume`. In this chapter's run, `fdatasync` took 5465 microseconds per flush; a local NVMe device would take well below a millisecond.
3. Check `pg_stat_wal` (`wal_sync`, `wal_sync_time` with `track_wal_io_timing = on`) for the flush count and time.

**Root cause.** Each commit requires one synchronous flush; the volume's flush latency bounds the number of commits per second per concurrent group.

**Fix.** Immediate: batch small writes into fewer transactions, and for non-critical writes set `SET LOCAL` `synchronous_commit = off` (accepting a loss window of a few hundred milliseconds). Permanent: place `pg_wal` on a low-latency device, and raise concurrency so that group commit amortises flushes (`commit_delay` and `commit_siblings` are available but rarely needed).

**Prevention.** Benchmark `pg_test_fsync` on every new volume type; verify that the storage honours flush requests (a volatile write cache without a battery silently breaks durability); keep a per-environment baseline of commit latency.

#### Incident: committed data lost after a crash

**Scenario.** To speed up an import, an operator set `fsync = off` and `synchronous_commit = off` in `postgresql.conf` and forgot to revert them. Weeks later the host lost power.

**Symptoms.** After the restart the latest minutes of orders are missing, or the server refuses to start with `invalid page` `in block ... of relation` or `could not locate a valid checkpoint record`.

**Diagnosis.** Check `SHOW fsync; SHOW synchronous_commit; SHOW full_page_writes;`, read the configuration history, and read the startup log for `redo` messages and page errors. `pg_controldata` shows the last checkpoint and cluster state.

**Root cause.** With `synchronous_commit = off` the acknowledgement precedes the log flush, so a crash loses the tail of the log (a bounded window, no corruption). With `fsync = off` the operating system may reorder or delay writes arbitrarily, and the cluster can be corrupted beyond recovery.

**Fix.** Immediate: restore from the latest backup and replay archived WAL (point-in-time recovery, covered in the chapter on backup); for a lost tail, re-ingest from the upstream source. Permanent: restore the defaults, and apply relaxed durability only per transaction (`SET LOCAL synchronous_commit = off`) for data that can be regenerated.

**Prevention.** Alert on non-default values of `fsync`, `full_page_writes` and `synchronous_commit` through configuration management; use `fsync = off` only for throwaway clusters, such as test fixtures, that are rebuilt from scratch.

#### Incident: periodic latency spikes from checkpoints

**Scenario.** Latency of a write-heavy service spikes every few minutes. The log contains `checkpoints are occurring` `too frequently`.

**Symptoms.** Spikes align with the lines `checkpoint starting: wal`; `pg_stat_bgwriter.checkpoints_req` grows faster than `checkpoints_timed`; WAL volume rises sharply after each checkpoint because of full-page images.

**Diagnosis.** Enable `log_checkpoints = on` (default on from PostgreSQL 15), compare `checkpoints_req` with `checkpoints_timed`, and measure the WAL rate with `pg_wal_lsn_diff` over a minute.

**Root cause.** `max_wal_size` is too small for the write rate, so WAL volume, not time, triggers checkpoints, each followed by a burst of full-page writes.

**Fix.** Raise `max_wal_size` (several GB is common for busy systems), leave `checkpoint_timeout` at 5 to 15 minutes and `checkpoint_completion_target` at 0.9, and consider `wal_compression = on` to shrink full-page images (off by default, as observed).

**Prevention.** Size `max_wal_size` to hold several minutes of peak WAL; keep an eye on recovery time, which grows with the checkpoint interval and the WAL volume.

### Questions to expect

blocks.title: Interview angle
blocks.text: Why is the log written before the data, and why is a commit fast although the data pages are not on disk? The log is sequential and small, so a flush is a single cheap write, and it contains enough information to redo the change after a crash. The data pages can be written later in any order, because recovery rebuilds them from the log. The write-ahead rule guarantees that no page reaches disk before its log records.

1. What is an LSN? A 64-bit position in the WAL stream; each page records the LSN of its last change, which enforces write-ahead and makes redo idempotent.
2. What does a checkpoint do and why does it matter for recovery time? It flushes dirty pages and records a redo point. Recovery replays only from that point, so the checkpoint interval and WAL volume bound recovery time.
3. What is a torn page and how is it handled? A partially written 8 kB page after a crash. PostgreSQL writes full-page images to WAL after each checkpoint; InnoDB uses the doublewrite buffer.
4. What does `synchronous_commit = off` risk? Loss of the most recent acknowledged transactions on a crash, without corruption. `fsync = off` risks corruption.
5. What are the phases of ARIES and which does PostgreSQL use? Analysis, redo, undo. PostgreSQL performs redo; uncommitted changes are invisible, so no undo pass is required.
6. How does `innodb_flush_log_at_trx_commit` compare? `1` flushes at each commit (durable), `2` writes at commit and flushes every second, `0` writes and flushes every second.
7. What does `kill -9` of a PostgreSQL backend cause? The postmaster terminates all backends and runs crash recovery; committed data is preserved, uncommitted data disappears.
8. Why can SSD or cloud storage break durability? A volatile cache that acknowledges flushes before the data is stable. The configuration must be tested with `pg_test_fsync` and verified with the provider.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
Key points

- WAL: log first, flush at commit, write data pages later; this makes commits cheap and crash recovery possible.
- Checkpoints bound recovery time; full-page writes protect against torn pages.
- PostgreSQL recovery replays redo only; uncommitted changes are discarded by visibility rules.
- `synchronous_commit = off` trades a bounded loss window for speed; `fsync = off` risks corruption and must not be used on real data.
- Measure flush latency and checkpoint frequency with `pg_test_fsync`, `pg_stat_wal` and `pg_stat_bgwriter`.

The guarantees of the previous chapters apply only to statements that actually run inside the intended transaction, on the intended connection, for the intended duration. In a Java service this depends on JDBC settings, on the connection pool, on the Spring proxy that implements `@Transactional`, and on the exceptions that leave a method. Most production transaction defects are not database defects: they are boundary errors in application code, such as a transaction annotation that is never applied, a rollback that never happens, or a transaction that stays open for the duration of a remote call.

This chapter describes the JDBC transaction API, the Spring declarative model with its propagation and rollback rules, the interaction with the connection pool, and the patterns for operations that span several databases or services: idempotency, the outbox and sagas. No JDBC driver or Spring artefact can be downloaded on the build machine, so Spring and JDBC listings are marked as not run; the proxy mechanism and the rollback rule were reproduced with plain Java programs that were run (JDK 21), and the SQL-level behaviour was verified on PostgreSQL 16.15.

### Concept and mechanism

#### JDBC transaction control

A JDBC `Connection` starts in autocommit mode. The transaction API consists of the following calls.

- `setAutoCommit(false)` begins an explicit transaction on the connection; the next statement opens it on the server.
- `commit()` and `rollback()` end it. `setSavepoint()` and `rollback(Savepoint)` provide partial rollback.
- `setTransactionIsolation(Connection.TRANSACTION_REPEATABLE_READ)` selects the level for subsequent transactions. Constants exist for the four standard levels.
- `setReadOnly(true)` is a hint that PostgreSQL turns into `SET TRANSACTION READ ONLY`.

A connection belongs to one thread at a time, and a transaction belongs to a connection. Everything that must be atomic has to run on the same connection between `setAutoCommit(false)` and `commit()`. A pool returns the connection with `close()`; a pool that finds an open transaction rolls it back (HikariCP does so unless the application already finished it).

#### Spring declarative transactions

Spring implements `@Transactional` with a **proxy**. When the container creates a bean whose class or methods carry the annotation, it wraps the bean in a proxy (a JDK dynamic proxy for interfaces, a CGLIB subclass otherwise). A call from another bean reaches the proxy first. The proxy asks the `PlatformTransactionManager` (for JDBC and JPA, `DataSourceTransactionManager` or `JpaTransactionManager`) to begin a transaction according to the attribute, binds the connection to the current thread, invokes the target method, and then commits or rolls back according to the outcome.

blocks.text:
Three consequences follow from this design and explain most surprises.

1. **Self-invocation.** A call such as `this.audit()` inside the bean skips the proxy, so annotations on `audit` have no effect.
2. **Visibility.** Only public methods invoked through the proxy are intercepted in the default proxy mode; `private`, `final` or `static` methods and a call from the constructor are not.
3. **Thread binding.** The connection is bound to a thread (`TransactionSynchronizationManager`). Work handed to another thread, such as `@Async`, a parallel stream or a `CompletableFuture`, runs outside the transaction.

#### Attributes: propagation, isolation, read-only, timeout

**Propagation** says what happens when a transactional method is called while a transaction already exists.

rows: Join the existing transaction, or start one if none exists.
Suspend the existing transaction and run in a new one on a new connection; commits or fails independently.
Run inside the existing transaction under a savepoint; failure rolls back to the savepoint (JDBC transaction managers only).
Join if one exists, otherwise run without a transaction.
Suspend any existing transaction and run without one.
Require an existing transaction; throw if none exists.
blocks.caption: Propagation values of Spring @Transactional (default REQUIRED).

blocks.text:
`REQUIRES_NEW` needs a second connection while the first is still held. With a small pool, nested `REQUIRES_NEW` calls from many threads at once can deadlock the pool itself, a point revisited in the incidents.

The `isolation` attribute issues the corresponding level at transaction start (the default, `DEFAULT`, uses the database default, READ COMMITTED on PostgreSQL and REPEATABLE READ on InnoDB). It takes effect only when the call starts a new transaction; a joined transaction keeps its level. `readOnly = true` allows optimisations (Hibernate skips dirty checking, PostgreSQL rejects writes) but does not make the code safe. `timeout` bounds the transaction duration in seconds.

#### Rollback rules

By default Spring rolls a transaction back when the method throws an unchecked exception (`RuntimeException` or `Error`), and commits when it throws a checked exception. This rule follows the EJB convention in which checked exceptions are treated as business outcomes. To change it, use `rollbackFor = Exception.class` or `noRollbackFor`. When a transactional method called through the proxy marks the shared transaction as rollback-only (for example because an inner `REQUIRED` method threw), the outer commit fails with `UnexpectedRollbackException`.

blocks.text:
#### Transaction boundaries and the connection pool

A pool such as HikariCP owns a fixed number of physical connections (`maximumPoolSize`, default 10) and lends them. With the default behaviour of the JDBC transaction manager, the connection is taken from the pool at the beginning of the transaction and returned at its end. The duration of the transaction is therefore the time during which the connection is unavailable to other threads. If the pool has 10 connections and each request holds a connection for 2 seconds while it waits for a remote service, the sustained capacity is 5 requests per second, regardless of how fast the database is. When all connections are in use, further callers wait for `connectionTimeout` (default 30 seconds) and then fail with `SQLTransientConnectionException`.

Two settings extend the lifetime unnoticed. With JPA, `spring.jpa.open-in-view` (default `true`) keeps the `EntityManager`, and under some configurations the connection, bound to the web request until the view is rendered, so lazy loading works in controllers but connections are held longer. Hibernate's `hibernate.connection.handling_mode` can release connections after each statement or after the transaction.

#### Idempotency, outbox and distributed work

A transaction covers one database. An operation that writes to a database and also publishes a message, calls another service or writes to a second store cannot be made atomic by `@Transactional` alone.

**Idempotency.** A retried request (after a timeout or a serialization failure) must not apply its effect twice. The usual technique is an idempotency key stored with a unique constraint: `INSERT INTO payment(idempotency_key, ...) ON` `CONFLICT (idempotency_key) DO NOTHING`, and the result of the first execution is returned to the retry.

**Transactional outbox.** The service writes the business row and an event row into an `outbox` table in the same local transaction. A separate relay process reads unpublished outbox rows (with `FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED`), publishes them to the broker and marks them as sent. Publication is at-least-once; consumers deduplicate by event id. This replaces a dual write, which can lose or duplicate messages, by one atomic local commit.

blocks.text: **Two-phase commit (2PC).** The classic protocol for atomic commit across several resource managers has a coordinator and participants. In phase one the coordinator asks each participant to **prepare**: it makes its changes durable and promises that it can commit. In phase two the coordinator decides and tells all participants to commit or to roll back. PostgreSQL exposes the participant side as `PREPARE TRANSACTION 'gid'`, `COMMIT PREPARED 'gid'` and `ROLLBACK PREPARED 'gid'`, with `max_prepared_transactions` set above its default of 0; JTA/XA implements the coordinator in Java.

blocks.text:
A prepared transaction survives a crash and keeps its locks and its hold on the vacuum horizon until resolved, so an abandoned one causes the bloat described in the chapter on MVCC. For this and for availability reasons, 2PC is rare between services.

**Sagas.** A **saga** replaces one distributed transaction by a sequence of local transactions, each with a **compensating** **action** that semantically undoes it (for example `CancelPayment` for `CapturePayment`). If step *n* fails, the compensations for steps *n-1* to 1 run in reverse. Sagas provide atomicity of outcome but not isolation: other transactions can see intermediate states, so designs add semantic locks (an order in state `PENDING`) and make every step and compensation idempotent.

### Worked example

The scenario is the self-invocation defect. `OrderService.placeOrder` is public and `@Transactional`; it calls `audit`, which is annotated `@Transactional(propagation = REQUIRES_NEW)` so that the audit row survives a rollback of the order. The expectation is that `audit` runs in its own transaction.

The following Java program reproduces the mechanism with a JDK dynamic proxy that logs when it would begin and commit a transaction. It is runnable on JDK 21 and stands in for the Spring proxy.

blocks.title: ProxyDemo.java

blocks.code:
$ java ProxyDemo.java
BEGIN before placeOrder
placeOrder body: A1
audit body: A1
COMMIT after placeOrder
---
BEGIN before audit
audit body: A1
COMMIT after audit
blocks.title: Run the proxy demonstration

blocks.text:
What to notice: the first call shows one `BEGIN` and one `COMMIT`, both for `placeOrder`; the `audit` body ran inside the transaction of `placeOrder` and received no transaction of its own. Only the second call, made from outside, passed through the proxy and began a transaction for `audit`. In Spring the same applies, so a `REQUIRES_NEW` annotation on a method called through `this` is ignored, and a rollback of `placeOrder` also removes the audit row.

### Hands-on

#### The rollback rule

The rule "roll back on unchecked, commit on checked" was verified with a runnable program that mirrors the default `TransactionAspectSupport` behaviour.

blocks.title: RollbackRule.java

blocks.code:
$ java RollbackRule.java
ROLLBACK (unchecked: IllegalStateException)
COMMIT (checked: IOException does not roll back by default)
ROLLBACK (unchecked: StackOverflowError)
COMMIT

#### Observing open transactions of a pool

When application threads hold transactions open, the database shows the same picture. Eight sessions executed `BEGIN` and a trivial query and then stayed idle, which is what a service does while waiting for a remote response.

**psql session (real output)**

blocks.code:
t=# SELECT state, count(*), max(now() - xact_start) > interval '0' AS has_open_tx
    FROM pg_stat_activity WHERE datname = 't' AND pid <> pg_backend_pid() GROUP BY state;
        state        | count | has_open_tx
---------------------+-------+-------------
 idle in transaction |     8 | t

t=# SELECT count(*) AS sessions, current_setting('max_connections') AS max_conn
    FROM pg_stat_activity WHERE backend_type = 'client backend';
 sessions | max_conn
----------+----------
        9 | 30

blocks.text:
Eight of the nine client sessions are `idle in transaction`. In a pool, each of them corresponds to a lent connection that does no database work.

### Real-world problems and solutions

#### Incident: connection pool exhaustion from open transactions

**Scenario.** A checkout endpoint is annotated `@Transactional` and, inside the method, calls a payment provider through HTTP. The provider slows down from 200 ms to 8 seconds. The pool holds 10 connections.

**Symptoms.** Latency rises on every endpoint of the service, including those that use no payment. The log contains `HikariPool-1 - Connection is not available, request timed out after 30000ms` (typical text; recent versions append `(total=10, active=10, idle=0, waiting=N)`). Database CPU is low.

**Diagnosis.**

1. Check the pool metrics: `hikaricp.connections.active` equal to the maximum and `hikaricp.connections.pending` greater than 0.
2. On the database, group sessions by state; the real output above shows the shape. In the failing case most sessions are `idle in transaction`.
3. Identify what they wait for: the `query` column shows the last statement, and `now() - state_change` shows how long they have been idle.

blocks.code:
SELECT pid, now() - state_change AS idle_for, left(query, 60) AS last_query
FROM pg_stat_activity
WHERE state = 'idle in transaction'
ORDER BY state_change
LIMIT 10;
blocks.title: idle_in_tx.sql

**Root cause.** The transaction boundary included a remote call, so connection hold time equalled the remote latency, and the pool capacity (10 divided by 8 seconds, about 1.2 requests per second) collapsed.

**Fix.** Immediate: add a client timeout and a circuit breaker for the provider; temporarily raise `maximumPoolSize` only if the database has headroom (a larger pool does not fix the cause and can overload the database). Permanent: restructure the method so that the transaction covers only the database work.

Because the two steps are no longer atomic, the charge call carries an idempotency key and a reconciliation job repairs orders that were charged but not marked.

**Prevention.** Set `idle_in_transaction_session_timeout` (for example 30 s), and statement and lock timeouts. Size the pool with the formula connections = (core count x 2) + effective spindle count as a starting point, and measure. Track connection hold time as a metric. A code rule: no network call inside a transaction.

#### Incident: @Transactional not applied (self-invocation)

**Scenario.** A developer annotates a private helper or a method called through `this` with `@Transactional(propagation` `= REQUIRES_NEW)` to write an audit row that must survive a failed order.

**Symptoms.** When the order fails, the audit row is missing as well. Or, a `@Transactional` method called from a scheduler inside the same class fails to roll back partial work; the log of `org.springframework.transaction` at `TRACE` shows no `Creating new transaction` line for the inner method.

**Diagnosis.**

1. Enable `logging.level.org.springframework.transaction.interceptor=TRACE` and `logging.level.org.springframework.orm.jpa=DEBUG`, and search for `Getting transaction for` and `Completing` `transaction for` around the call.
2. Verify that the call crosses a bean boundary: if the caller and callee are in the same class, the proxy is bypassed, as in the demonstration above.
3. Confirm at runtime with `TransactionSynchronizationManager.isActualTransactionActive()` and `getCurrentTransactionName()` inside the method.

**Root cause.** The annotation is implemented by a proxy; a call through `this` never reaches it.

**Fix.** Move the method to another bean (the simplest and most robust option), or inject the proxy of the own bean, or use `TransactionTemplate` programmatically for the block:

blocks.title: AuditWriter.java (fragment, not run)

blocks.text:
AspectJ mode (`@EnableTransactionManagement(mode = AdviceMode.ASPECTJ)`) weaves the advice into the class and removes the limitation at the cost of build-time or load-time weaving.

**Prevention.** Cover every transactional behaviour that the business depends on with an integration test that checks the database state after a forced failure; make `@Transactional` visible only on public methods of service beans.

#### Incident: rollback does not happen on a checked exception

**Scenario.** A service method debits an account and then throws a checked `PaymentDeclinedException` to signal a business failure.

**Symptoms.** The exception reaches the controller, the customer sees an error, but the debit remains in the database.

**Diagnosis.** With `TRACE` logging on `org.springframework.transaction.interceptor`, the log shows `Completing` `transaction for [...]` followed by a commit rather than `Completing transaction for [...] after exception`. A unit test with an embedded database that asserts the balance after the exception fails.

**Root cause.** The default rule commits on checked exceptions, as shown by the real output of `RollbackRule`: `COMMIT` `(checked: IOException does not roll back by default)`.

**Fix.** Use `@Transactional(rollbackFor = PaymentDeclinedException.class)` or `rollbackFor = Exception.class` as a project default. Alternatively make the exception unchecked.

**Prevention.** Adopt a convention: business exceptions extend `RuntimeException`, or every service annotation carries `rollbackFor = Exception.class`. Review catch blocks: an exception that is caught inside the transactional method (for example to log it) also prevents the rollback, unless the code calls `TransactionAspectSupport.currentTransactionStatus().setRollbackOnly()` or rethrows.

#### Incident: long transaction spanning a batch job

**Scenario.** A nightly job loads one million rows, processes each one and updates it, all in a single `@Transactional` method.

**Symptoms.** The transaction runs for two hours; table bloat grows, replication lag increases because the replica applies the changes in one burst at commit, locks held on updated rows block the daytime application, and a failure at row 900 000 rolls everything back.

**Diagnosis.** `pg_stat_activity` shows one session with `xact_start` hours old, and the horizon is held back (see the chapter on MVCC). `pg_locks` shows many row locks held by the same pid.

**Root cause.** The transaction boundary equals the job rather than a unit of work.

**Fix.** Process in chunks of a few hundred to a few thousand rows, each in its own transaction (a `TransactionTemplate` per chunk, or Spring Batch chunk-oriented steps), record the last processed key so that the job can be resumed, and make each chunk idempotent.

**Prevention.** Limit transaction duration through `transaction_timeout` (PostgreSQL 17 and later) or `statement_timeout`, and review jobs for unbounded transactions.

### Questions to expect

blocks.title: Interview angle
blocks.text: How does @Transactional work, and when does it silently fail? Spring wraps the bean in a proxy that begins a transaction, binds the connection to the thread, calls the method, and commits or rolls back. It fails silently when the call does not pass through the proxy (self-invocation, private or final methods), when the work moves to another thread, when the bean is not managed by Spring, and when a checked exception is thrown without `rollbackFor`.

1. What is the default rollback rule? Roll back on `RuntimeException` and `Error`, commit on checked exceptions. `rollbackFor` and `noRollbackFor` change it.
2. Difference between `REQUIRED`, `REQUIRES_NEW` and `NESTED`? `REQUIRED` joins or starts; `REQUIRES_NEW` suspends the current transaction and uses a second connection and a separate commit; `NESTED` uses a savepoint inside the same transaction.
3. How can a pool of 10 connections be exhausted by a database that is idle? Transactions that stay open while waiting for something else hold connections. The database sees `idle in transaction`.
4. Why should a remote call not occur inside a transaction? It extends connection and lock hold time to the remote latency and couples the failure of the remote system to the pool and the database.
5. What is the outbox pattern? The event is written to a table in the same transaction as the business data and published by a relay afterwards, giving at-least-once delivery without a distributed transaction.
6. Why is two-phase commit rarely used between services? Participants block holding locks while awaiting the coordinator, the coordinator is a single point of failure, and latency grows; sagas with compensations are preferred.
7. What is idempotency and how is it implemented for payments? Repeating a request has the same effect as running it once; an idempotency key with a unique constraint stores the first result and returns it to retries.
8. What does `spring.jpa.open-in-view` change? It keeps the persistence context open for the whole request, enabling lazy loading in the view, at the cost of longer connection use and queries outside service boundaries. Many production setups disable it.
9. How does `isolation = SERIALIZABLE` change the code? Serialization failures (SQLSTATE 40001) must be retried around the whole transaction, outside the transactional method, for example through `@Retryable` placed on a caller bean.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
Key points

- A Spring transaction is a thread-bound connection managed by a proxy; calls that bypass the proxy get no transaction.
- Default rollback is on unchecked exceptions only; use `rollbackFor` for business exceptions.
- Transaction duration equals connection hold time; never include remote calls or user waits inside a transaction.
- Use idempotency keys, the outbox and sagas instead of distributed transactions between services.
- Serialization failures and deadlocks require a retry of the whole transaction on a fresh connection.

A database connection is not a lightweight handle. It is an authenticated session with its own memory, its own transaction state and, in PostgreSQL, its own operating-system process. A Spring Boot service that opens a connection for every request spends more time connecting than querying, and a fleet of services that each open hundreds of connections can exhaust the server long before the CPU is busy. This chapter explains what a connection costs, how a pool bounds that cost, how JDBC talks to the server, and why prepared statements are both a performance feature and the only reliable defence against SQL injection.

### Concept and mechanism

#### Process per connection versus thread per connection

PostgreSQL forks one backend process for every client connection. The postmaster process listens on the port, authenticates the client, and forks a backend that serves that session until it disconnects. Each backend has private memory (catalog caches, sort and hash memory governed by `work_mem`, prepared statement plans) and attaches to the shared memory segment that holds `shared_buffers`, the WAL buffers and the lock tables. MySQL with InnoDB uses one thread per connection inside a single `mysqld` process; threads are cheaper to create than processes, and a thread cache reuses them, but each thread still holds session buffers and a stack.

blocks.text: The consequences are the same in both engines. Connection establishment involves a TCP handshake, optional TLS negotiation, authentication and session initialisation. Measured on the build machine with `pgbench` (select-only, four clients, local socket), persistent connections sustained about 46 970 transactions per second at 0.085 ms average latency, while opening a new connection for every transaction (`pgbench -C`) sustained 233 transactions per second at 17.2 ms average latency, of which 8.3 ms was connection time. The query is identical in both runs; only the connection handling differs.

blocks.code:
$ pgbench -S -c 4 -j 2 -T 10 pgb
latency average = 0.085 ms
tps = 46968.644072 (without initial connection time)
$ pgbench -S -C -c 4 -j 2 -T 10 pgb
latency average = 17.153 ms
average connection time = 8.265 ms
tps = 233.192396 (including reconnection times)
blocks.title: Persistent versus per-transaction connections (measured, typical)

blocks.text:
#### max_connections and why more is not better

`max_connections` (default 100 in PostgreSQL; the experiments in this chapter use 30) is a hard ceiling. A fraction of it, `superuser_reserved_connections` (default 3), is kept for administrators so that a saturated server can still be diagnosed. When ordinary clients exceed the remaining slots, PostgreSQL refuses the connection immediately:

blocks.code:
$ psql -U appuser shop -c "select 1"
psql: error: connection to server on socket ".../.s.PGSQL.20500" failed:
FATAL:  remaining connection slots are reserved for roles with the SUPERUSER attribute
$ psql -U postgres shop -c "select 1 as superuser_still_ok"
 superuser_still_ok
--------------------
                  1
blocks.title: Connection refusal when the ordinary slots are used (real output)

blocks.text: Raising `max_connections` is rarely the correct fix. Throughput is bounded by the hardware, not by the number of sessions. The measurement below drove a TPC-B-like workload (`pgbench` default script) against a server with two CPU cores. Throughput peaked at four clients and then fell, because additional sessions only add context switching and lock contention. The figures are noisy because the build machine is shared, but the shape is the general behaviour.

blocks.text:
#### Connection pools

A connection pool keeps a fixed set of established connections and lends them to request threads. A request borrows a connection, runs its statements, and returns the connection; the physical session stays open. HikariCP is the default pool in Spring Boot. Its central setting is `maximumPoolSize`: the maximum number of connections, idle plus in use. When all connections are borrowed, further requests wait up to `connectionTimeout` (30 000 ms by default) and then fail with an exception.

blocks.text: The key HikariCP settings are listed below. Values are the documented defaults.

rows: Upper bound of connections (idle plus active).
Idle connections kept ready; the documentation recommends leaving it unset for a fixed-size pool.

blocks.caption: HikariCP settings that matter in production.

blocks.text: In Spring Boot these are set with the prefix `spring.datasource.hikari`:

blocks.code:
spring.datasource.url=jdbc:postgresql://db.internal:5432/shop
spring.datasource.username=shop_app
spring.datasource.hikari.maximum-pool-size=10
spring.datasource.hikari.connection-timeout=5000
spring.datasource.hikari.max-lifetime=1740000
spring.datasource.hikari.leak-detection-threshold=20000
blocks.title: application.properties

blocks.text:
A connection timeout of 5 000 ms instead of 30 000 ms makes an exhausted pool fail fast and visibly rather than piling up request threads.

#### Sizing the pool

The widely cited formula from the PostgreSQL and HikariCP guidance is a starting point, not a result:

**pool sizing starting point**

blocks.code: connections = (core_count * 2) + effective_spindle_count

blocks.text:
For a database server with 4 cores and one SSD this gives about 9 connections for the whole database, shared by every application instance. The formula is derived from the observation in the measurement above: the number of useful concurrent sessions is bounded by cores plus the time sessions spend waiting for I/O. The practical procedure is:

1. Determine the database budget: `max_connections` minus the reserved slots minus the connections of administrative tools, replicas and migration jobs.
2. Divide the budget by the number of application instances at their maximum scale (including the extra instances present during a rolling deployment).
3. Set `maximumPoolSize` to that figure, and verify under load that the pool wait time (Hikari metric `hikaricp.connections.pending`) stays near zero.

With 20 application pods and a database budget of 80 connections, each pod receives 4 connections. A pool of 10 per pod would request 200 connections and exceed the limit, which is the mechanism behind the connection storm described later in this chapter.

#### An external pooler: PgBouncer

When many instances or many short-lived processes (serverless functions, batch jobs) need access, an external pooler such as PgBouncer multiplexes many client connections onto few server connections. In transaction pooling mode a server connection is assigned to a client only for the duration of one transaction, which allows thousands of clients to share a few dozen backends. The price is that session state does not survive between transactions: `SET` commands without `LOCAL`, session-level advisory locks, `LISTEN` and, in older versions, server-side prepared statements cannot be relied upon. Session pooling mode keeps the full semantics but multiplexes less.

### Worked example: JDBC from first principles

JDBC is the standard Java API for relational databases. The sequence is always the same: obtain a `Connection`, create a `PreparedStatement`, bind parameters, execute, read a `ResultSet`, close everything (try-with-resources closes in reverse order). The following class is a complete service method in plain JDBC. It requires the PostgreSQL JDBC driver on the class path, which is not available on the build machine; the listing is therefore not run here, and the SQL it sends was executed through `psql` in the sections that follow.

blocks.title: CustomerDao.java

blocks.text:
What to notice: `DriverManager.getConnection` opens a new physical connection on every call, which is exactly the per-request cost measured above. In a Spring application the `DataSource` (HikariCP) replaces `DriverManager`, and `con.close()` returns the connection to the pool instead of closing the socket. The parameter marker `?` is the essential line: the statement text and the values travel separately.

### Hands-on: SQL injection and the fix

The following demonstration uses real PostgreSQL 16 on the build machine. A login check is written by concatenating strings. The Java program below builds the three statements that the vulnerable code would send for three different inputs; it was run with the source launcher.

blocks.title: Inject.java

blocks.code:
$ java Inject.java
SELECT id, name, is_admin FROM customers WHERE email = 'c5@example.com' AND password = 'pw5'
SELECT id, name, is_admin FROM customers WHERE email = 'c5@example.com'
  AND password = 'x' OR '1'='1'
SELECT id, name, is_admin FROM customers WHERE email = 'c5@example.com'; DROP TABLE orders;
  --' AND password = 'x'
blocks.title: Output of the program (the three statements)

blocks.text: The second statement changes the logic: `AND` binds tighter than `OR`, so the condition becomes `(email = ... AND` `password = 'x') OR '1'='1'`, which is true for every row. Executing it in `psql` returns the whole table, administrator first:

blocks.code:
shop=# SELECT id, name, is_admin FROM customers WHERE email = 'c5@example.com'
shop-#   AND password = 'x' OR '1'='1';
  id  |     name      | is_admin
------+---------------+----------
    1 | Customer 1    | t
    2 | Customer 2    | f
    3 | Customer 3    | f
    4 | Customer 4    | f
    5 | Customer 5    | f
    6 | Customer 6    | f
blocks.title: Executing the second statement

blocks.text: The third statement terminates the first query and appends a second one. The simple query protocol accepts several statements in one message, and the demonstration table was actually destroyed:

blocks.code:
$ sed -n 3p out.txt | psql shop -f -
 id |    name    | is_admin
----+------------+----------
  5 | Customer 5 | f
(1 row)

DROP TABLE
shop=# select count(*) from orders;
ERROR:  relation "orders" does not exist
blocks.title: Executing the third statement (real output)

blocks.text: The fix is a parameterised statement. The server receives the statement text with placeholders first (Parse), then the values (Bind). The values are never part of the parsed SQL, so no quote character can change the structure. The same behaviour can be demonstrated in `psql` with `PREPARE`:

blocks.code:
shop=# PREPARE login(text, text) AS
shop-#   SELECT id, name, is_admin FROM customers WHERE email = $1 AND password = $2;
PREPARE
shop=# EXECUTE login('c5@example.com', 'x'' OR ''1''=''1');
 id | name | is_admin
----+------+----------
(0 rows)
shop=# EXECUTE login('c5@example.com', 'pw5');
 id |    name    | is_admin
----+------------+----------
  5 | Customer 5 | f
(1 row)
blocks.title: Parameterised statement with the malicious value (real output)

blocks.title: Watch out
blocks.text: Parameters protect values, not identifiers. A table name, column name or `ORDER BY` direction cannot be a `?` parameter. For a dynamic sort column, map the user input to a fixed allow-list (`switch` on known names) and append the mapped literal; never append the raw input. Spring Data JPA derived queries and `Sort` objects validate property names against the entity, which is why they are safe for this case, whereas a native query concatenating `ORDER BY` + `sortParam` is not.

#### Prepared statements and plan caching

A prepared statement is parsed once and can be executed many times. The PostgreSQL JDBC driver switches to a server-side prepared statement after `prepareThreshold` executions (default 5). The server then keeps a named statement per connection; for the first five executions of a statement it plans with the actual parameter values (custom plans), after which PostgreSQL may switch to a cached generic plan if it is not estimated to be worse. Prepared statements are per connection, which is why PgBouncer transaction pooling historically needed care with them.

#### Batch inserts

Each statement sent in autocommit mode is its own transaction and costs a WAL flush and a network round trip. The measurement below loaded 20 000 rows into a table with a serial key using four methods, all against a local socket; on a real network the round-trip share is larger, so the relative gap grows.

blocks.code:
single INSERT per statement, autocommit:        28.6 s
single INSERT per statement, one transaction:    0.91 s
20 multi-row INSERTs of 1000 rows, one txn:      0.126 s
COPY from a CSV file:                            0.082 s

blocks.text: In JDBC the corresponding technique is `addBatch()` and `executeBatch()` inside one transaction. The PostgreSQL driver can rewrite a batch of inserts into a multi-row statement when the property `reWriteBatchedInserts=true` is set on the URL. In Spring Data JPA, `saveAll` with `spring.jpa.properties.hibernate.jdbc.batch_size=50` and `spring.jpa.properties.hibernate.order_inserts=true` enables Hibernate batching; note that a `GenerationType.IDENTITY` key disables insert batching in Hibernate, whereas `SEQUENCE` with an allocation size permits it.

blocks.title: BatchInsert.java

blocks.text:
### Real-world problems and solutions

#### Incident: FATAL too many connections after scaling out

**Scenario.** An order service runs 6 pods with the Spring Boot default pool of 10. Traffic grows and the platform autoscaler adds pods. The database allows 100 connections, of which administrative tooling and a reporting job use 15.

**Symptoms.** Intermittent errors in the application log: `FATAL: sorry, too many clients already` or `remaining` `connection slots are reserved for roles with the SUPERUSER attribute`. New pods fail their readiness probe. Existing requests succeed, so the outage looks partial.

**Diagnosis.** Count sessions by state and by application, from a superuser connection (the reserved slots make this possible):

blocks.title: diagnosis.sql

blocks.code:
state               | count
---------------------+-------
 idle                |    71
 idle in transaction |    12
 active              |     4
blocks.title: Typical output during the incident (shape of the data)

blocks.text:
Most sessions are `idle`: pools hold connections that no request is using. The few `idle in transaction` sessions point to code that begins a transaction and then waits (a remote call inside `@Transactional`).

**Root cause.** Total demand is `pods * maximumPoolSize` = 10 pods \* 10 = 100, plus 15 external users, which exceeds `max_connections`. The sessions are mostly idle, so the pool size is far larger than the concurrency the database can use (see the throughput measurement above).

**Fix.** Immediate: lower `maximumPoolSize` to 4 on all pods (a configuration change and rolling restart), terminate idle sessions of the reporting job. Permanent: compute the per-pod pool from the budget (the procedure above), add PgBouncer in transaction mode if the number of pods must grow, and set `idle_in_transaction_session_timeout` so that sessions stuck inside a transaction are released.

**Prevention.** Alert at 80 percent of `max_connections`; load-test with the maximum pod count; include the rolling-update surge in the budget.

#### Incident: connection storm after a deployment

**Scenario.** A deployment restarts all pods at once. Each new pod eagerly opens its full pool and warms caches by running queries; old pods are still draining.

**Symptoms.** For about 30 seconds after the rollout starts the database refuses connections, latency spikes on queries that were healthy, and the application reports pool timeouts.

**Diagnosis.** `pg_stat_activity` grouped by `backend_start` shows a burst of sessions created in the same seconds; `log_connections` confirms the rate. Compare the number of pods during the rollout with the connection budget.

**Root cause.** The rolling update strategy allowed `maxSurge` extra pods and each pod opens `minimumIdle` (equal to `maximumPoolSize` by default) connections at start. During the overlap there are more pods than the budget assumed. Authentication of many simultaneous sessions also consumes CPU.

**Fix.** Immediate: pause the rollout, scale old pods down only after new pods are ready. Permanent: lower the pool size, set `maxSurge` to a small number, start the pool lazily (`initializationFailTimeout` and a small `minimumIdle`), and place PgBouncer between the services and the database so the server sees a stable number of connections.

**Prevention.** Rehearse deployments in a staging environment that has the real connection limit.

#### Incident: SQL injection through a search endpoint

**Scenario.** A product search builds `"SELECT * FROM products WHERE name LIKE '%" + q + "%'"` in a repository method using `JdbcTemplate.query(String)`.

**Symptoms.** The access log shows requests with `q=' UNION SELECT email, password, null FROM customers --`; the response contains customer emails. Alternatively errors such as `syntax error at or near "'"` appear for ordinary input containing an apostrophe (for example the name O'Brien), which is the benign symptom of the same defect. **Diagnosis.** Search the code for string concatenation into SQL: `grep -rn "\" *+" src | grep -i` `"select\|update\|delete"`. Search the database log (`log_statement = 'all'` temporarily, or `log_min_error_statement`) for statements containing `UNION` or `--` that no code path should generate.

**Root cause.** User input reaches the SQL text. The application account was also over-privileged: it could read the `customers` table although the search feature needs only `products`.

**Fix.** Immediate: take the endpoint offline or block the pattern at the gateway, rotate credentials that may have been exposed. Permanent: use `?` placeholders (`jdbcTemplate.query(sql, mapper, "%" + q + "%")`), or a Spring Data derived query `findByNameContainingIgnoreCase`; restrict the role with `GRANT SELECT ON products` only (see the chapter on security).

**Prevention.** Static analysis (SpotBugs with Find Security Bugs, or CodeQL) in CI, code review rule against concatenated SQL, least-privilege roles so that an injection has little to read.

### Questions to expect

#### What does a database connection cost and why do we pool?

Each connection is a server process (PostgreSQL) or thread (MySQL) with private memory and, on creation, a TCP handshake, optional TLS and authentication. Measured here, reconnecting for every transaction reduced throughput from about 47 000 to 233 transactions per second. A pool amortises the cost by reusing established sessions and bounds the number of sessions the database must serve.

#### How large should a HikariCP pool be?

Small: start near `cores * 2 + spindles` for the whole database and divide it among application instances. Throughput stops improving at a small multiple of the core count; beyond that, requests should queue in the application where waiting is cheap. Verify with pool wait metrics.

#### Why is a PreparedStatement safe against SQL injection?

The statement text is parsed and planned before the values arrive; values are bound as typed data. A quote inside a value cannot end a string literal because there is no literal to end. This protects values only; identifiers must be validated against an allow-list.

#### What is the difference between `connectionTimeout`, `maxLifetime` and `idleTimeout`?

`connectionTimeout` is how long a caller waits for a connection from the pool. `maxLifetime` retires a connection after a maximum age (to avoid stale connections closed by firewalls or the database). `idleTimeout` retires idle connections above `minimumIdle`.

#### Why can `GenerationType.IDENTITY` hurt batch inserts?

Hibernate must read the generated key immediately after each insert, so it cannot defer and group the statements. A sequence with an allocation size lets Hibernate assign keys in memory and batch the inserts.

#### What does transaction pooling in PgBouncer break?

Anything that relies on session state spanning transactions: session-level `SET`, session advisory locks, temporary tables and `LISTEN`.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
- A connection is an expensive server-side session; reconnecting per transaction cost a factor of about 200 in the measurement.
- Pools should be small; the database connection budget is divided among all instances, including deployment surge.
- Parameterised statements separate code from data and are the only reliable defence against SQL injection; identifiers need allow-lists.
- Group statements: one transaction instead of autocommit, then batches or `COPY`, cut a 20 000-row load from 28.6 s to under 1 s.
- `idle in transaction` sessions and leaked connections are the usual cause of pool exhaustion.

A single database server is a single point of failure and a single point of capacity. Replication keeps additional copies of the data on other servers. The copies serve three purposes: survival of a server loss (high availability), additional read capacity (read replicas) and a source for backups or analytics. Replication also introduces the most common source of subtle production defects in database-backed applications: a copy that is slightly behind the original.

### Concept and mechanism

#### Physical and logical replication

PostgreSQL streaming replication is physical: the standby receives the write-ahead log (WAL) of the primary, the byte-level record of every change to every page, and replays it. The standby is therefore an exact copy of the whole cluster, same major version, and it cannot accept writes while it follows. Logical replication decodes the WAL into row changes (INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE) per table and publishes them to subscribers; the subscriber is an independent, writable database that may have a different schema, version or additional tables. Logical replication is the tool for selective replication, zero-downtime major upgrades and change data capture; physical replication is the tool for high availability.

MySQL replication is logical in the sense that it ships the binary log (binlog) of committed transactions, in row, statement or mixed format, and the replica re-executes them through an applier thread. MySQL deployments use GTIDs (global transaction identifiers) to identify each transaction, which makes it possible to repoint a replica to a new source without computing file positions.

blocks.text:
#### The streaming protocol in PostgreSQL

A commit writes WAL records to the WAL buffers and then flushes them to the local `pg_wal` directory. A walsender process on the primary reads WAL and sends it over a TCP connection to the walreceiver on the standby. The standby writes the received WAL to its own disk (`write_lsn`, `flush_lsn`) and the startup process replays it into the data files (`replay_lsn`). Queries on a hot standby see the state as of the last replayed position.

blocks.text:
#### Synchronous and asynchronous replication

By default replication is asynchronous: the primary acknowledges a commit after its own WAL flush and streams to the standby afterwards. If the primary is lost, the most recent transactions may not have reached the standby and are lost on failover. Setting `synchronous_standby_names` makes the commit wait until the named standby has confirmed the WAL (according to `synchronous_commit`; the value `on` waits for the standby flush, `remote_apply` waits for replay). Synchronous replication gives a recovery point objective of zero for committed transactions at the price of commit latency, and it turns a standby outage into a primary outage unless several candidates are listed.

blocks.text:
#### Replication lag and read-your-writes

Replication lag is the time or the amount of WAL between the primary's latest position and the position a replica has replayed. When an application routes reads to a replica, it may read a state older than its own last write. This violates read-your-writes consistency: a user updates a profile, is redirected, and sees the old profile. Approaches are: read from the primary for a short window after a write (a session flag), wait on the replica for a given LSN before reading (`pg_last_wal_replay_lsn()` compared with the LSN returned by `pg_current_wal_lsn()` at commit), use synchronous `remote_apply` for the few operations that need it, or accept staleness for views where it is harmless (catalogue pages, dashboards).

### Worked example: streaming replication on one machine

Two PostgreSQL 16 clusters were created: the primary on port 20500 with `wal_level = replica`, and a standby cloned from it with `pg_basebackup`. The `-R` option writes `standby.signal` and the connection settings into `postgresql.auto.conf`; `-C -S` creates a physical replication slot named `replica1_slot`; `-X stream` includes the WAL needed to make the copy consistent; `-c fast` requests an immediate checkpoint (without it the base backup can wait for a spread checkpoint).

blocks.code:
$ pg_basebackup -h /tmp/osw_d5 -p 20500 -D /tmp/osw_d5/replica \
    -R -X stream -C -S replica1_slot -c fast -P -v
49568/49568 kB (100%), 1/1 tablespace
pg_basebackup: write-ahead log end point: 0/80001B0
pg_basebackup: syncing data to disk ...
pg_basebackup: base backup completed
$ cat replica/postgresql.auto.conf
primary_conninfo = 'user=postgres ... host=''/tmp/osw_d5'' port=20500 ...'
primary_slot_name = 'replica1_slot'
$ pg_ctl -D replica -l replica.log -w start

### Hands-on: lag, synchronous commit and promotion

#### Creating measurable lag

Replay on the standby was paused with `pg_wal_replay_pause()`, a row was inserted on the primary, and the standby was queried. The WAL had arrived (received LSN advanced) but had not been replayed.

primary=# insert into customers(id,name,email)
primary-#   values (5001,'Late Writer','late@example.com') returning id;
5001
standby=# select id,name from customers where id=5001;
 id | name
----+------
(0 rows)

primary-#   pg_wal_lsn_diff(sent_lsn, replay_lsn) as replay_gap_bytes from pg_stat_replication;

sent_lsn         | 0/9002C10
replay_lsn       | 0/9000060

blocks.text:
Spring routing to replicas is usually implemented with a `AbstractRoutingDataSource` that selects a pool by the `readOnly` flag of the current transaction (`@Transactional(readOnly = true)` goes to the replica). The mechanism is sound, but it makes every read-only transaction subject to the lag described above; an operation that must see its own write should not be marked `readOnly`.

#### Synchronous commit

The standby registers with the default `application_name walreceiver`. After `ALTER SYSTEM SET` `synchronous_standby_names = 'walreceiver'` and a reload, the standby is reported as synchronous and commits wait for it. With the standby up the commit took 0.17 s through `psql`; with the standby stopped the commit never returned.

blocks.code:
$ psql shop -c "select application_name, state, sync_state from pg_stat_replication"
 application_name |   state   | sync_state
------------------+-----------+------------
 walreceiver      | streaming | sync
$ pg_ctl -D replica -m fast -w stop
server stopped
$ timeout 5 psql shop -c "insert into customers(id,name) values (5003,'sync blocked')"
$ echo $?
124
primary=# select pid, state, wait_event_type, wait_event from pg_stat_activity
primary-#   where wait_event = 'SyncRep';
 pid  | state  | wait_event_type | wait_event
------+--------+-----------------+------------
 4510 | active | IPC             | SyncRep
blocks.title: Commit waits when the synchronous standby is down (real output)

blocks.text: The transaction is already durable on the primary (the row became visible locally) but the client has no acknowledgement. Cancelling the wait yields a warning that the transaction was committed locally but may not be replicated. The setting was reset with `ALTER SYSTEM RESET synchronous_standby_names`.

blocks.title: Gotcha
blocks.text: Synchronous replication with a single standby couples availability. If the only synchronous standby fails, every commit blocks. Production configurations list at least two candidates, for example `ANY 1 (standby_a, standby_b)`, so that one failure does not stop writes.

#### Promotion and split brain

Failover replaces a failed primary with a standby. `pg_ctl promote` (or `SELECT pg_promote()`) ends recovery and starts a new timeline. On the build machine promotion took 0.23 s. Because the old primary was still running and reachable, both servers then accepted writes for the same key:

blocks.code:
$ pg_ctl -D replica -w promote
server promoted
$ psql -p 20501 shop -c "select pg_is_in_recovery()"
 pg_is_in_recovery
-------------------
 f
$ psql -p 20501 shop -c "insert into customers(id,name) values (7001,'written on NEW primary')"
INSERT 0 1
$ psql -p 20500 shop -c "insert into customers(id,name) values (7001,'written on OLD primary')"
INSERT 0 1
$ psql -p 20501 shop -tA -c "select pg_walfile_name(pg_current_wal_lsn())"
000000020000000000000016
$ psql -p 20500 shop -tA -c "select pg_walfile_name(pg_current_wal_lsn())"
000000010000000000000016
$ cat replica/pg_wal/00000002.history
1       0/1665E3E0      no recovery target specified
blocks.title: Two primaries (real output)

blocks.text: The first eight hex digits of the WAL file name are the timeline: the promoted node is on timeline 2, the old primary is still on timeline 1. The history file records the point where timeline 2 branched. Both servers now contain a row with key 7001 and different content: this is split brain. Nothing in the databases themselves prevents it.

blocks.text:
Prevention is external to the database: a failover manager (Patroni with a consensus store such as etcd, repmgr with a witness) that promotes only with a quorum, and fencing of the old primary (power or network isolation, or demoting it before routing traffic) before the new primary is announced. The old primary must be rebuilt as a standby, with `pg_rewind` (requires `wal_log_hints = on` or data checksums) or with a new base backup.

### Real-world problems and solutions

#### Incident: stale reads after a write

**Scenario.** A Spring Boot service routes `@Transactional(readOnly = true)` methods to a replica. After checkout, the order confirmation page calls `getOrder(id)` and returns 404 for about one request in two hundred.

**Symptoms.** The order exists when queried a few seconds later. Support tickets say "my order disappeared". The failures cluster around batch jobs that write heavily.

**Diagnosis.** On the primary, `SELECT application_name, replay_lag, pg_wal_lsn_diff(sent_lsn, replay_lsn) AS` `gap_bytes FROM pg_stat_replication;` shows replay lag growing during the batch. On the replica, `SELECT now() -` `pg_last_xact_replay_timestamp();` gives the age of the replayed data (it is also non-zero on an idle primary, so interpret it together with the first query). Compare with the failing request time.

**Root cause.** Asynchronous replication plus read routing: the read after the write ran on a replica that had not replayed the commit. Replay also lags when a long query on the replica conflicts with WAL replay (`max_standby_streaming_delay`).

**Fix.** Immediate: route the confirmation read to the primary. Permanent: read-your-writes policy (primary for N seconds after a write by the same session, or LSN wait), alerts on `replay_lag` above a threshold, and keep long analytical queries on a dedicated replica with a larger delay allowance or `hot_standby_feedback` tuned deliberately.

**Prevention.** Mark only genuinely lag-tolerant reads as read-only and replica-routed; test with an artificially delayed replica (`recovery_min_apply_delay` on a test standby).

#### Incident: failed failover and split brain

**Scenario.** A network partition isolates the primary from the failover manager. The manager promotes a standby; the old primary keeps running and the application tier still holds connections to it.

**Symptoms.** Customer reports show different data depending on the request; unique-key violations appear when replication to a rebuilt standby is attempted; the old primary's replication connections have disappeared from `pg_stat_replication`.

**Diagnosis.** On each node run `SELECT pg_is_in_recovery();` and `SELECT` `pg_walfile_name(pg_current_wal_lsn());`. Two nodes answering `f` with different timeline numbers confirm split brain. Compare the divergent rows (as in the demonstration above).

**Root cause.** The old primary was not fenced before promotion, and clients were not forced to the new primary.

**Fix.** Immediate: stop the old primary (or block its client traffic), choose the authoritative node, export the writes made only on the other node (the difference of the two datasets) for manual reconciliation. Permanent: rebuild the loser as a standby from the winner, and run a failover manager with quorum-based leadership and fencing.

**Prevention.** Failover drills; a single connection endpoint (virtual IP, DNS with a short TTL or a proxy) that is switched as part of the fenced promotion.

#### Incident: disk full because of WAL growth from an inactive replication slot

**Scenario.** A standby was shut down for maintenance and never returned. Its replication slot remained on the primary. The `pg_wal` directory grows until the volume fills.

**Symptoms.** Monitoring shows the data volume filling at the rate of write activity; eventually the primary logs `PANIC:` `could not write to file "pg_wal/xlogtemp..."` and stops. Nothing is wrong with the tables themselves.

blocks.text:
**Root cause.** A replication slot guarantees that the primary keeps all WAL the slot's consumer has not yet received. With the consumer gone, `restart_lsn` does not advance, and every change since then is retained.

**Fix.** Immediate: if the standby is not coming back, drop the slot with `SELECT` `pg_drop_replication_slot('replica1_slot');` and the next checkpoint recycles the WAL. If the standby must be kept, bring it back. Permanent: set `max_slot_wal_keep_size`, which bounds the retained WAL. With `max_slot_wal_keep_size = 64MB` the server invalidated the slot at the next checkpoint:

blocks.code:

DETAIL:  The slot's restart_lsn 0/9002D38 exceeds the limit by 150983368 bytes.
HINT:  You might need to increase max_slot_wal_keep_size.
   slot_name   | active | wal_status | restart_lsn | safe_wal_size
---------------+--------+------------+-------------+---------------
 replica1_slot | f      | lost       |             |

blocks.text:
The standby, restarted afterwards, failed with `requested WAL segment 000000010000000000000009 has already been` `removed`. It caught up after a `restore_command` pointing to the WAL archive was added, which is the reason to keep an archive in addition to a slot (see the chapter on backups). **Prevention.** Alert on `pg_replication_slots` where `active = false` and on retained bytes; alert at 70 percent disk usage of the WAL volume; set `max_slot_wal_keep_size` to a value smaller than the free space.

#### Incident: replica lag grows without bound

**Scenario.** A reporting query of two hours runs on the replica. The standby falls minutes behind and stays behind.

**Symptoms.** `replay_lag` rises; the replica logs `canceling statement due to conflict with recovery`, or, with `hot_standby_feedback = on`, the primary shows bloat.

**Diagnosis.** `SELECT * FROM pg_stat_database_conflicts;` on the replica, `pg_stat_replication` on the primary, and the settings `max_standby_streaming_delay` and `hot_standby_feedback`.

**Root cause.** WAL replay must remove row versions that the long query still needs. The standby either cancels the query after `max_standby_streaming_delay` (default 30 s) or delays replay. With feedback the primary retains the old versions instead.

**Fix.** Separate analytical replicas from failover replicas, tune the delay for the analytical one, or move the report to a materialised view refreshed on the primary.

**Prevention.** Monitor replay lag per replica and give reporting a replica of its own.

### Questions to expect

#### Physical versus logical replication?

Physical replication ships WAL pages for the whole cluster; the standby is a byte-identical read-only copy of the same major version. Logical replication ships decoded row changes per table through publications and subscriptions; the subscriber is writable and may differ in version and schema. Use physical for high availability, logical for selective replication and upgrades.

#### What does asynchronous replication risk?

Loss of acknowledged transactions on failover: the primary acknowledges the commit before the standby has the WAL. Synchronous replication removes that loss at the cost of commit latency and of coupling availability to the standby.

#### What is split brain and how is it prevented?

Two nodes both believe they are the primary and accept writes. Prevented by quorum-based leader election, fencing the old primary before promotion, and a single controlled client endpoint.

#### How do you handle read-your-writes with replicas?

Route the reading request to the primary after a write for a time window, wait for the replica to replay the writer's LSN, or use synchronous `remote_apply` for critical flows. Avoid replica reads for data that the same user has just changed.

#### What does a replication slot do and why is it dangerous?

It makes the primary retain WAL until the consumer has received it. An abandoned slot retains WAL indefinitely and fills the disk; bound it with `max_slot_wal_keep_size` and alert on inactive slots.

#### What is a timeline?

A numbered branch of WAL history. Promotion starts a new timeline, recorded in a history file, so that WAL from the old and new branches cannot be confused.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
- Physical replication copies WAL for high availability; logical replication copies row changes for selective use and upgrades.
- Asynchronous replication is fast but loses recent commits on failover; synchronous replication does not, but blocks commits if the standby disappears.
- Read replicas serve stale data by design; the application must define which reads tolerate lag.
- Promotion is quick (0.23 s here); safety comes from fencing and quorum, not from the promote command.
- An inactive replication slot retains WAL without limit; set `max_slot_wal_keep_size` and alert.

Replication protects against the loss of a server. It does not protect against the loss of data: a `DELETE` without a `WHERE` clause, a faulty migration or a corrupting application bug is replicated to every standby within milliseconds. Protection against logical damage requires backups, and a backup is only worth the restore that has been tested. This chapter compares logical and physical backups, performs both on a real PostgreSQL 16 server, and recovers from an accidental mass delete to a chosen point in time.

### Concept and mechanism

#### Logical and physical backups

A logical backup (`pg_dump`, `mysqldump`, `mysqlpump`) reads the data through SQL and writes the statements, or an archive of them, that recreate the objects and rows. It is portable across versions and operating systems, can restore a single table, and produces a consistent snapshot of one database (it runs in one `REPEATABLE READ` transaction). Restoring re-executes the inserts and rebuilds every index, so its duration grows with data volume. A physical backup copies the data files (`pg_basebackup`, Percona XtraBackup, filesystem or storage snapshots). It restores at the speed of file copy, includes all databases, and is tied to the same major version and architecture. Combined with archived WAL (PostgreSQL) or binary logs (MySQL) it supports point-in-time recovery.

blocks.text:
#### RPO and RTO

The recovery point objective (RPO) is the maximum acceptable amount of data loss, measured in time; the recovery time objective (RTO) is the maximum acceptable duration of the outage. A nightly dump gives an RPO of up to 24 hours. A base backup plus continuous WAL archiving gives an RPO of the archive delay (seconds, bounded by `archive_timeout` and segment switching). RTO is determined by restore speed and, for point-in-time recovery, the amount of WAL to replay. Both are properties of a rehearsed procedure, not of the configuration.

blocks.text:
#### Point-in-time recovery in PostgreSQL

PostgreSQL archives WAL segments with `archive_command` (any command that copies `%p`, the segment path, to safe storage under the name `%f`). A base backup defines the starting state; recovery starts from the base backup, fetches WAL with `restore_command`, replays it, and stops at a recovery target (`recovery_target_time`, `recovery_target_lsn`, `recovery_target_xid` or a named restore point created with `pg_create_restore_point`). The server is told to enter recovery by an empty file `recovery.signal` in the data directory. `recovery_target_action = 'promote'` makes it open for writes when the target is reached.

MySQL has the equivalent procedure: restore a full backup, then replay the binary logs up to a position or time with `mysqlbinlog --stop-datetime=... | mysql`. The mechanism requires `log_bin` enabled and the binary logs retained (`binlog_expire_logs_seconds`); the commands below for MySQL are typical and were not run on the build machine.

### Worked example: logical dump and restore

The sample database `shop` (customers and 200 000 orders, 24 MB on disk) was dumped in two formats. The custom format (`-Fc`) is compressed and supports selective and parallel restore; the plain format is a SQL script.

blocks.code:
$ time pg_dump -Fc -f dumps/shop.dump shop        # 0.77 s
$ ls -l dumps/shop.dump | awk '{print $5}'
2196136
$ time pg_dump -Fp -f dumps/shop.sql shop         # 0.32 s
$ ls -l dumps/shop.sql | awk '{print $5}'
10601932
$ grep -n -E "^(CREATE TABLE|COPY|ALTER TABLE ONLY)" dumps/shop.sql | head -6
29:CREATE TABLE public.customers (
44:CREATE TABLE public.orders (
80:ALTER TABLE ONLY public.orders ALTER COLUMN id SET DEFAULT nextval(...);
87:COPY public.customers (id, name, email, is_admin, password) FROM stdin;
1099:COPY public.orders (id, customer_id, amount, status, created_at) FROM stdin;
201114:ALTER TABLE ONLY public.customers
blocks.title: pg_dump in custom and plain format (real output; sizes in bytes)

blocks.text: The ordering in the script is deliberate: tables, then data through `COPY`, then constraints and indexes, because loading data into an unindexed table and building the index afterwards is much faster than maintaining the index per row. `pg_restore -l` lists the table of contents of the custom archive, which can be edited to restore a subset (`-L`).

blocks.code:
$ createdb shop_restored
$ time pg_restore -j 2 -d shop_restored dumps/shop.dump      # 0.95 s
shop_restored=# select (select count(*) from customers) c,
shop_restored-#   (select count(*) from orders) o;
  c   |   o

### Hands-on: base backup, WAL archive and recovery from an accidental

### DELETE

#### Setup

The primary was configured with `archive_mode = on` and `archive_command = 'cp %p /tmp/osw_d5/archive/%f'`. A production archive command must be atomic and idempotent (copy to a temporary name and rename, never overwrite), and should write to storage outside the database server. A base backup was taken with `pg_basebackup` and verified with `pg_verifybackup`, which checks the backup manifest:

blocks.code:
$ pg_basebackup -D /tmp/osw_d5/base1 -X stream -c fast
$ pg_verifybackup /tmp/osw_d5/base1
backup successfully verified
$ du -sh base1
88M     base1
blocks.title: Base backup (real output)

blocks.text:
#### The accident

After the backup, 500 more orders were inserted. The time `T0` (06:59:46.461 UTC) was noted as the last good moment. Two seconds later a `DELETE FROM orders` was executed without a `WHERE` clause, the classic mistake of a console session pointed at production. A WAL segment switch (`pg_switch_wal()`) made sure the segment holding the delete reached the archive.

blocks.title: The mistake (real output)

blocks.text:
#### The recovery

The base backup was copied to a new directory (the pg\_wal contents were left out, because recovery takes WAL from the archive), and recovery was configured in the new copy. The damaged production server was not touched, so the recovered copy could be inspected before anything was changed.

port = 20501
archive_mode = off
restore_command = 'cp /tmp/osw_d5/archive/%f %p'
recovery_target_time = '2026-10-18 06:59:46.461+00'
recovery_target_action = 'promote'
